content: 1. Comprehensive healthcare services for individuals with HIV, those in prison health systems, drug dependence treatment programs, outreach services, and needle and syringe programs (NSPs) should include core components that have been proven feasible in these settings. Adherence to treatment should be supported through measures such as monetary incentives and concurrent opioid substitution therapy (OST) when necessary, ideally provided at the same location. 2. Guidelines exist for intensified tuberculosis (TB) case-finding and isoniazid preventive therapy for people living with HIV in resource-limited settings. These also include psychosocially assisted pharmacological treatment for opioid dependence, management of latent TB infection, and recommendations for investigating contacts of individuals with infectious TB in lowand middle-income countries. Collaborative TB/HIV activities are guided by WHO policies for national programs and stakeholders. 3. Infection control measures are critical to prevent TB transmission in healthcare facilities and congregate settings. HIV and TB programs should provide managerial direction at national and subnational levels to implement TB infection control. Each facility should have a TB infection-control plan integrated into the general infection-control strategy, supported by stakeholders, and include administrative, environmental, and personal protection measures. Surveillance of TB among workers is also essential. 4. Healthcare workers, community health workers, and care providers living with HIV should receive antiretroviral therapy (ART) and isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) if eligible. They should also be offered opportunities to work in clinical sites with minimal TB transmission risk. Workers in contact with TB patients, people living with HIV, and people who inject drugs (PWID) should assess risk factors for HIV and viral hepatitis and provide comprehensive prevention and service information. They must also protect themselves from occupational exposure to TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis. 5. Congregate settings, such as healthcare facilities, sex work venues, drug treatment centers, shelters, and prisons, often lack basic TB infection-control measures. These environments increase TB exposure risks, especially for PWID, due to crowded conditions and untreated active TB cases. The HIV epidemic exacerbates TB risks among healthcare workers, prisoners, and those in police or military barracks. Improving access to HIV and TB prevention, treatment, and care services for healthcare workers and those in congregate settings is essential. 6. Implementing TB infection-control measures requires managerial activities at national, subnational, and facility levels. These include establishing coordinating bodies, developing infection-control plans, designing appropriate healthcare facilities, conducting TB surveillance among workers, and implementing advocacy and communication strategies. At the facility level, administrative, environmental, and personal protection controls aim to reduce TB transmission risks. 7. Administrative controls include providing care outside congregate settings, triaging individuals with TB symptoms, isolating infectious cases, promoting respiratory hygiene, ensuring rapid TB diagnosis and treatment, and minimizing hospitalization. Environmental controls involve optimizing ventilation systems and using ultraviolet germicidal irradiation where applicable. Personal protective measures include respirators and comprehensive care packages for healthcare workers, including ART and IPT for those living with HIV. 8. ART should be initiated for all adults and adolescents living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count. Priority should be given to those with severe or advanced HIV disease or CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³. ART should also be provided in settings offering OST, and opioid agonists can be administered alongside medical treatment for TB, hepatitis, or HIV without requiring opioid abstinence. 9. Alcohol dependence, active drug use, and mental health issues should not be barriers to HIV or TB treatment for PWID. ART is the most effective strategy to reduce TB incidence among people living with HIV, but access remains disproportionately low for PWID. Decentralizing ART initiation and maintenance to OST settings and community-based services can improve adherence and outcomes. 10. Early ART initiation improves clinical outcomes for people living with HIV compared to delayed treatment. WHO recommends ART for all individuals living with HIV, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, regardless of CD4 count. Efavirenz-based fixed-dose combinations are preferred for first-line ART, including for individuals with TB, hepatitis B, or co-infections. 11. HIV testing services (HTS) should be routinely offered to all patients with presumptive or diagnosed TB and their partners. Community-based HTS linked to prevention, care, and treatment services is recommended for PWID. Provider-initiated testing and counseling should be available in generalized epidemics across all healthcare settings and in concentrated epidemics for services addressing STIs, hepatitis, TB, and PWID. 12. Knowledge of one’s HIV status is fundamental to accessing prevention, care, and treatment services. Early HIV identification in individuals with TB is critical for fast-tracking ART. HTS should be available in TB services, NSPs, drug treatment centers, prisons, and community settings. TB diagnosis offers an entry point for PWID and their contacts to access HIV care and other life-saving services, such as OST, NSP, ART, and viral hepatitis management. 13. Observational studies show that testing TB patients and their contacts for HIV leads to high rates of new HIV diagnoses due to the higher prevalence in these groups. Voluntary HTS for sexual or needle-sharing partners, with mutual disclosure, is essential to prevent further transmission.
